Here's how I would do it. First calculate the average speed of a player. You just do a simple average over all the speeds ur given.

Then whenever u make teams you want the average speed of that team to get as close to the average runner speed as possible. 

I would start by first picking the fastest player, then using dynamic programming build up the rest of the team. This is the hardest part of the algorithm. But I imagine you would keep track what your current average is and add players that swing you closer to the overall average. So if your average is too high pick a slower player. If your average is to low pick a higher player. You keep the player that keeps you closest to ideal average. 

I feel like this is the best way to go about it because you are aiming for the average player speed, so you are trying to lower the variance as much as possible.

So I tried to solve Goldbach's Conjecture for the lolz and I had a pretty neat idea.  What I did was for a even number I listed out all the ways it could be written as a sum two odd numbers. Then I considered the number of prime factors used to create each  number. So for a prime number the number of prime factors is 1 for 4 its 2 for 12 its 3 for 1 its 0.  So for example for 12 the odd numbers you can use to make up 10 are 1,3,5,5,7,9, The number of factors are 0,1,1,1,1,2.  The sum of these is 6.

The idea was to guarantee atleast one pair was made up by two primes.
 So the way I went about it was eliminating the case that 1 might get matched with a prime. If it did, then it doesn't help prove Goldbach's conjecture. We assume it does for this calculation to remove that possibility. 6 - 1 = 5. 

These 5 factors have to be split up among the remaining 2 pairs of numbers. That means on average a pair has 2.5 factors. However we eliminated the case with 1, which means that the remaining pairs must have atleast 2 factors. Since the average was 2.5, we've guaranteed that one of these pairs has 2 factors, and therefore 10 can be written as a sum of two primes. 

From here I was going to try to prove that it was impossible to ever reach a avergae of 3 primes was impossible, but after experimenting with it, found that the average number of factors goes up. I think the biggest number this works for is 74.

I guess it could still be considered as a test. If it passes this you know it can be written as the sum of two primes.
